_comment: The main story (issue #18, scripts/story.gd). speakers and talks use the same format as data/dialogue.json and are merged into it by Dialogue.data(), so Dialogue.talk("ch1_arrest") works anywhere. beats: what plays in Hollowmark, checked in order every time Ash is in town; the first beat whose conditions hold and whose talk has not been seen plays. A beat: talk (id), when (conditions, see Story.meets: active (a campaign started with the story on), cleared, not_cleared, seen, joined, renown, held, day), pick instead of talk (issue #186: the climax betrayal picks the talk, letter or scene, see Betrayal.beat_talk), then (what happens after the talk: launch:<mission id>, command_on, act1_end, open_region:<region id> to lift the fog over a region of the territory map; several can be joined with commas), card ([title, subtitle] shown after the talk). goals: the story checklist, shown in the journal's Quests tab (I, issue #114) under the chapter they belong to: text, chapter (a chapter id from data/journal.json), hint, done (conditions), show (conditions; hidden until they hold).

ch1_arrest.title: Chapter 1  ·  No Such Person
lines: Hollowmark: a wall, a well, a few hundred people pretending the horizon is not getting closer. Bran walks you in through the south gate like a man delivering a parcel he has not been paid for yet.
bran
Right. Tax office first. Everyone who comes through 'ere gets written down. Then we find out what you're worth.
clerk
Next. Name?
You say nothing. You have nothing to say it with.
clerk
Name, please. For the Ledger.
bran
Ash. Put Ash. Ash, of nowhere, occupation: lucky.
smug
clerk
There is no Ash in the Ledger. There is nobody of nowhere in the Ledger. There is, in fact, nothing at all where you are standing.
surprised
clerk
I regret the Concord cannot process you. And anything the Concord cannot process is, per statute, a violation.
warden
Existing without authorization. Come along.
bran
Hey. Hey! That's my discovery. I found that. I got a prior claim!
angry
The cell is small, clean, and has a window exactly the size of a person who will never fit through it. Night comes down. Somewhere to the east, the Blank hums to itself.
Then the humming gets closer.

ch1_breakout_intro.title: Chapter 1  ·  No Such Person
lines: A key scrapes in the lock. The east wall of the tax office is... not there anymore. Just white, eating its way along the stone like frost.
bran
Evening. Don't get up on my account. Actually, do get up, the building's being eaten.
bran
Breakin' you out's a service. Services cost money. You'll pay me later, when you got some. With interest.
smug
bran
Wardens are still more scared of paperwork than of the Blank, so they'll try to stop us. Put 'em down, mind the Nibblers, and we walk out the front like taxpayers.

ch1_recaptured.title: Chapter 1  ·  No Such Person
lines: The wardens drag you back to the cell. It is smaller than you remember. The Blank is louder.
bran
That was a practice run. This time, try 'itting the ones in uniform.
angry

ch1_takeover.title: Chapter 1  ·  No Such Person
lines: Dawn. The square is full of people in nightclothes, staring at the place where the tax office used to be. It is a neat white hole now, with a few desks at the edge, still being filed.
At the rim of the white stands a woman in a pale archivist's coat, hands folded, watching it eat. She notices you. She does not look surprised. She looks interested.
verity
Oh. So you are the one it gave back. How rude of it. It never gives anything back, you know.
verity
I'm sorry about the building. Well. Not very. Do you know how many families that office struck out of the Ledger for being three coins short?
sad
verity
We shall speak again, I should think. You have the look of someone who is about to be rather inconvenient.
She steps backward into the white, and the white closes behind her like a door.
governor
Out of my way! The Ledger shall hear of this, I say! I shall be writing reports for a decade!
angry
Governor Thale's carriage rattles out of the north gate at a speed carriages are not built for. He takes the town seal with him. He does not take the town.
quill
Well. Hollowmark now has no governor, no tax office and no legal standing. Per Concord law, nobody may run it.
quill
And you, according to the Ledger, are nobody. I hate how well that works.
smug
tobble
Oh, that's grand. Nobody running the place. Half the town's been wishing for that for years.
happy
bran
I'm 'earing 'unregistered town with no tax collector.' I'm 'earing a business opportunity.
smug
quill
There's a table in the square with a map of the Inklands pinned to it. The governor used it to decide who to tax. You could use it to decide who to save.
Somebody has to hold the line. Everyone in the square turns, slowly, to look at the one person who legally isn't there.

act1_rumours.title: Act 1  ·  The Unregistered Town
lines: tobble
Word travels when a town loses its governor. Two bits of it might interest them as isn't running Hollowmark.
tobble
First: there's a hedge-witch in the Gutterwoods, selling cures out of a hollow tree. The Coven wants her gone. A town with no healer could do worse.
smug
tobble
Second: a Concord corporal walked out on an Erasure order and is hiding along the Tithe Road. Nine fingers. Ten opinions. The Concord's put a price on their head.
quill
Rumours like that show up as Rescue jobs on the Guildhall board, or as Rescue missions on the territory map if you'd rather fetch them yourself.
bran
A 'ealer and a deserter. Now we're a real outfit. A real, illegal outfit.
happy

act1_writ.title: Act 1  ·  The Concord Answers
lines: quill
A Concord rider nailed this to the well. I'll read it in the voice it deserves.
angry
quill
'By order of the Office of Audits: the unregistered settlement of Hollowmark has failed to file. A tithe column will assess it at Old Mill Crossing and collect all outstanding sums.'
bran
Collect what? We don't owe 'em nothin'. We don't even exist.
surprised
quill
That's the outstanding sum, as it were. Us.
ninefingers
Know that column. Tithe-Captain Morrow. Counts people the way other men count sheep. Meet him at the Crossing before he reaches the gate.
gristle
Bring him back alive if you can. A tonic I've got, been dying to try it on a tax man.
smug
ninefingers
Not yet. Morrow marches with forty wardens and assesses every hamlet on the way. Gives us a few days. Go now, we're a footnote.
quill
Then we stop being a footnote. Four provinces under the flag and enough Renown that the Concord has to spell our name right. Then we go and meet him.

act1_concord_intro.title: Act 1  ·  The Concord Answers
lines: captain
Halt. You there, the one standing where nobody's written. You'll do as a first entry.
captain
Hollowmark owes the Concord eleven months of tithe, a governor, a tax office and a full apology, duly assessed. We'll take it in coin, grain or people.
bran
How about none of the above, and you walk home lighter?
smug
captain
Wardens! Assess them.

act1_concord_after.title: Act 1  ·  The Concord Answers
lines: The tithe column is broken. Its strongbox was empty: they came to fill it. Among Morrow's papers is an order stamped with a red quill.
ninefingers
That seal. Seen it twice. Both times, the town it was stamped on stopped being a town by morning.
sad
quill
The Auditor. The Concord doesn't send him to collect. It sends him to strike things out of the Ledger. Streets. Families. Whole towns.
quill
He's marching down the Tithe Road. If he reaches Hollowmark with that quill, we won't be erased by the Blank. We'll be erased by paperwork.
angry
bran
Then we meet 'im on the road. Somebody check what a giant pen is weak to.
gristle
Whole, nobody walks away from that quill. Beds I want first. Bandages, a roof, a stove for the kettle. An Infirmary, Ash.
angry
quill
And make some noise while she builds it. The Ledger can strike out a town nobody's heard of. A town people sing about takes paperwork. Fifteen Renown, say.
ninefingers
He walks. Stops at every tollgate to check the books. We have time. Not much.

act1_end.title: End of Act 1
lines: Three days after the Auditor falls, a letter arrives. Nobody delivered it. It is simply on the Command Table one morning, weighed down with a smooth white stone.
letter
'To whoever is running Hollowmark, which I understand is nobody:'
letter
'Congratulations on the Auditor. He struck out four towns I was fond of, and I could never quite reach him. You have saved me a great deal of trouble.'
letter
'I want you to understand that I am not your enemy. I am the person who has read the drafts. When you have read them too, I think we will agree about the Concord.'
letter
'Please stop pushing the white back. It is only trying to help. Fondly, and with regret for what comes next: V. Hale.'
quill
She has lovely handwriting. I'd like to set it on fire.
angry
bran
Polite letters are the worst kind. Means they already decided.
sad
Outside, the Blank hums against the edges of the map. Hollowmark holds. For now, that is enough.
That night every bell in the north begins to ring at once, and does not stop. By morning the fog over Saint Ledger's has lifted, as if something up there wants to be found.

ch2_bells.title: Chapter 2  ·  The Copying Monks
lines: The bells have rung for three days. Every hour, all at once, from the hills in the north. The dogs of Hollowmark have stopped barking back.
On the fourth morning a monk walks in at the south gate in sandals worn down to string. He asks for whoever is in charge. Everyone points at you, then looks embarrassed.
odo
Brother Odo, of Saint Ledger's. I was sent to the Concord for help. The Concord sent me back with a receipt.
odo
So I came to the person the Concord is most annoyed with. Brother Cellarer said that was practical. Brother Cellarer is blank now. Or dead. We are not sure which.
quill
Saint Ledger's keeps the second copy of the Ledger. Every name, every deed, every debt. If the capital's copy burned, the monks would write the world back.
odo
We would. We are trying. The Abbot has us copying day and night. He has every hour rung at once, so that no brother sleeps through his turn.
odo
And the pages come out blank. We write, and the ink sinks into the paper and does not come back up. Some brothers have started copying the blank pages. Very carefully.
bran
So the monks have gone mad and the bells won't shut up. What's that to us?
odo
Candleford makes our candles. Without candles we copy in the dark. And the Erasers are burning the wax barges on the lake.
ninefingers
Erasers. White coats, tapers. Read the names out before they light a fire. Verity's lot. Saw one burn a tithe barn once. Read every name off the door first. Very polite.
odo
They say the Abbey's books are lies, and they may be right. But if the books burn, the brothers who are still written in them go too.
quill
Candleford is free land on the lake. Nobody has claimed it. Save the barges and the town will owe you. Towns that owe you are my favourite kind of town.
bran
Monks pay late. Write that down, Quill.
quill
Filed, as it were.

ch2_candleford_intro.title: Candleford
lines: Candleford smells of tallow and smoke. Out on the lake a barge is burning with a clean white flame that gives off no heat at all.
nell
You! Are you the Abbey's? No, you've got boots on. Good. Get down to the jetty before they light the last one.
nell
Nell Tapper. I make the candles. I also run the town, since the reeve ran off with the strongbox. Two jobs. No wages.
bran
Who's lightin' 'em?
nell
White coats. They read out a list of names at every barge and then set it going. Whose names, I asked. Ones you never heard of, they said. That's the point, they said.

ch2_candleford_outro.title: The Last Barge
lines: The last barge rocks at the jetty, scorched down one side, its wax sweating in the sun. Out on the lake the white flames go out one at a time.
nell
One barge. One out of six. The Abbey will say I owe them five.
nell
Right. You saved it, so you get a say. Whoever holds Candleford, I'll keep the wicks coming. Put somebody sensible in the reeve's chair and the Abbey gets its wax.
Pinned to a jetty post with a taper is a list of names in a careful hand. At the bottom it says: 'Read at Candleford, for those the Ledger forgot. Askew, First Reader.'
bran
Nice writin'. I hate 'em already.

ch2_candleford_after.title: Wax for the Abbey
lines: A wax barge reaches Saint Ledger's, and for one night the Abbey's windows are lit. The bells keep ringing. Brother Odo comes back down the north road with a letter sealed in red.
odo
From Prioress Ebba. The Abbot does not write letters any more. He says letters are copies, and copies are his business.
quill
Ahem. 'Saint Ledger's thanks Candleford's new keeper for the wax. The Abbey will receive the keeper once Candleford is properly governed, and not before. We do not deal with towns run by passers-by.'
bran
Passers-by. We saved their candles.
ninefingers
Fair, though. Town with no governor is a town with nobody to blame. Put a name in the chair.
quill
Post a governor in Candleford from the Governors screen. The Prioress wants someone to blame, and frankly so do I.

ch2_hall_ready.title: An Invitation
lines: odo
Your governor sent the Prioress a list of the Abbey's unpaid candle bills. She was furious. Then she invited you.
odo
Come to the Abbey, she says. Come armed. The cloister walk is not safe after dark, and it is always dark now.
gristle
Monks asking for visitors to come armed. Lovely, that is. I'll bring the good bottles, shall I?
smug

ch2_hall_intro.title: Saint Ledger's
lines: The Abbey gate stands open. Candles burn in every niche of the cloister walk, and between them the stone is going white in patches, like damp.
ebba
You are the passer-by. I am Prioress Ebba. I keep the house while the Abbot keeps the books.
ebba
The copying hall is through the walk. Three lecterns, forty brothers who will not stop writing, and things in the walk that used to be brothers.
ebba
Light the candles at the lecterns and the copyists will see what they write. Perhaps then they will notice it is nothing.
bran
And the things in the walk?
ebba
They do penance. With their hands. Do not let them touch your face. They wipe off what they touch.

ch2_hall_abbot.title: The Copying Hall
lines: The candles catch. In the copying hall forty monks sit at forty desks, writing fast. Every page in front of them is blank. Every page stacked behind them is blank. Nobody looks up.
At the head of the hall a tall old man in a black habit dips a quill and writes on the air. Where he writes, the air goes white.
wulfstan
Prioress. You have let in a draught.
ebba
Father Abbot, this is the keeper of Candleford. They brought the wax.
wulfstan
Good. Then they may copy. Sit. There is a desk. There is always a desk.
wulfstan
The capital's Ledger is going. Did they tell you? Page by page. When it is gone, ours is the world. So we copy. We copy the copy. We copy ourselves, if we must.
bran
Your pages are blank, mate.
wulfstan
Then the world is blank, and we shall copy that faithfully too. Fidelity is the whole of the Rule.
He turns back to the air. The Prioress takes your arm and walks you out, quickly, without looking at the desks.
ebba
He wrote the first new hymn this house had sung in a hundred years. Now he writes the hours on the air and calls it the Office.
ebba
Someone may know why the ink will not hold. Sister Osyth kept the crypts under the Bonefield Cloister. The Erasers took the Bonefield a month ago. Nobody has heard from her since.
ebba
Bring her out and the Abbey will owe you. I do not say that lightly. We owe the Concord already, and look where it got us.

ch2_hall_after.title: Taxed as Pasture
lines: quill
I looked up the Bonefield Cloister in my old Concord books. Per the Ledger, the hill was always empty. No cloister, no graves. Taxed as pasture.
quill
Which is odd, because there is a cloister on it. I have a drawing.
ninefingers
Erasers hold it. Camp at the top, fires going day and night. Form E-1: enemy dug in. Form E-2: enemy smug about it.
bran
Dig an old nun out from under an Eraser camp. That's hazard pay, that is. On the bill.

ch2_hild.title: Sister Hild
lines: abeyance
Oh. You've been to the Abbey. You smell of it. Beeswax and wet stone and the Abbot's ink, which is made with something I never asked about.
abeyance
I left because the page started writing back. The Abbot used to say a scribe's hand belongs to the Rule. Mine kept wandering off.
abeyance
The voices have been louder since you said the word Bonefield. Hundreds of them. Very polite. They keep asking who is counting them.
abeyance
Sister Osyth counted them, I think. She still is, probably. Do bring her back. She was horrible to me for six years, God keep her, and I miss her.

ch2_crypt_intro.title: The Bonefield
lines: The Bonefield Cloister sits on a bald hill. The Erasers have pitched white tents in the ruined garth, and a book-pyre burns in front of the chapel without any smoke.
askew
Visitors. Welcome. I am Askew, First Reader. You are the one the Blank gave back, and you have come to stop us burning things. That's sweet.
askew
Before you start, will you hear a name? We read them before every fire. Hollin Marsh, aged six, struck out for her father's debts. There. Now somebody has said it.
ninefingers
Heard that list before. Doesn't make your fire any less of a fire.
askew
No. But it makes it an honest one. Readers! The Unwritten wants to argue.

ch2_osyth.title: The Crypt-Keeper
lines: The ossuary is lined floor to ceiling with skulls in neat rows. Every row has a chalk number. An old nun with a board on a string is chalking the next one.
osyth
Eleven thousand four hundred and four. Don't jog my elbow.
osyth
You'll be the noise upstairs. Took you long enough. The Erasers sealed me in a month back, and the Blank's been at the bottom rows since.
osyth
Eleven thousand four hundred and five. The Concord says this hill was always empty. I've been counting the empty for forty years.
bran
Time to go, Sister.
osyth
Not till I've counted the last of them. They're behind the Founders' Door. Hold the stair while I open it, and keep your feet off the numbers.

ch2_verity.title: The Unedited Page
lines: Behind the Founders' Door is a small chamber with one stone shelf. On it sits a single skull, smaller than the others. A woman in a pale archivist's coat sits on the floor beside it, reading.
verity
Hello again. Please don't hit anything. The ceiling is very old and I am very tired.
osyth
Eleven thousand four hundred and six. That's all of them.
verity
Thank you, Sister. You are the only person who has ever got the number right. The Concord's own drafts say eleven thousand. They rounded.
verity
I brought you something. I thought you should see it before you decide whose side the Abbey is on.
She holds out a page. Unlike every page in the copying hall, this one is full: columns of names in an old clerk's hand, and across the top a heading struck through with one neat line.
verity

The Bonefield Rising. Three hundred years ago this valley refused a tithe. The Concord answered. Afterwards it struck the valley out of the Ledger, and the monks built their Abbey on top and copied a Ledger that said the hill was always empty.
verity
Every page they have copied since rests on this one. That is why the ink will not hold, I should think. It is sitting on eleven thousand people it was told to forget.
ninefingers
Ink doesn't care about history. You're telling stories.
verity
I am reading drafts. It is my profession. It was.
bran
So what d'you want? You ain't come all the way down 'ere for a chat.
verity
I wanted you to know what you are defending when you defend their books. That is all. I do not want to fight you. I rather like you. It is going to make next year very difficult.
She stands and brushes off her coat. Then she looks past you at the dark corner of the chamber and tilts her head, as if someone there had said something she did not quite catch.
verity
Yes. In a moment.
She walks into the wall. For a breath the wall is white, and then it is a wall again.
osyth
She left the count alone. Good. I'd have had words.

ch2_verity_after.title: Several Abbots
lines: osyth
Your table's crooked. I'll see to it. First, the Abbot.
osyth
I told the Prioress what's under the Bonefield. She went white. Then she went to tell the Abbot, and he locked the copying hall and started copying himself.
quill
Copying himself. In what sense?
osyth
In the sense that there's four Abbots in the hall now, all writing. One's real. The others are very good copies.
ninefingers
Put down the real one and the copies stop. Standard.
osyth
The Prioress won't let outsiders near her Abbot till the Abbey trusts you. Earn it. Gifts, trade, whatever they ask for. Then come back with a sharp stick.
quill
The Abbey's standing is on the Diplomacy screen. Monks, it turns out, respond to money and to candles in roughly equal measure.

abbot_intro.title: The Abbot Who Copied Himself
lines: The copying hall has emptied into the cloister garth. The forty desks stand in the wet grass. Among the yews, men in black habits walk in step, each with a crozier, each writing on the air.
ebba
Father Wulfstan. Father. Please. It is Ebba.
wulfstan
Prioress. Which of us are you speaking to? We are all the Abbot. I made certain. If the first copy fails, there is the second.
wulfstan
The Bonefield. Yes. The sister told you. I knew. Every abbot knows. We copy the empty hill so that it stays empty. That is the Office.
wulfstan
And now the ink will not hold. So I shall hold it. Faithfully. Forever. Several of me.
bran
Only one of 'em bleeds. The rest is paper.
ebba
Watch his hands. The real one's hands are always inky. He never in his life wrote clean.

abbot_phase2.title: The Second Copy
lines: The Abbot staggers. Ink runs out of his sleeves onto the grass. Around the garth every copy stops, turns, and looks at him at once.
wulfstan
Half. You have struck out half of me. Then the other half shall be copied twice as carefully.
ebba
He is calling the penitents in from the walk. And mind the gold leaf: when he illuminates, get well back.

abbot_outro.title: Blank Paper
lines: The copies crumple one after another, until the garth is littered with blank sheets the shape of an old man. The real Abbot kneels among them with one sheet held to his chest.
wulfstan
I copied it so carefully. Every hill. Every empty hill.
ebba
I know, Father.
wulfstan
Prioress. Count them for me. Someone should.
He does not get up again. The bells stop. After a while one of them starts again, on the hour, alone.

ch2_end.title: The House Keeps Silence
lines: Saint Ledger's bells ring the hours one at a time again. In the copying hall the brothers have stopped writing. Some of them are asleep at their desks for the first time in a month.
ebba
We buried him by the Founders' Door, with the eleven thousand. He would have hated that. He would also have understood it.
ebba
The Abbey will not copy the Ledger any more. We are going to copy Sister Osyth's board instead. All of it, with the heading put back.
osyth
Took three hundred years. Spelling had better be right.
ebba
The Concord will call this treason. The Erasers will call it too little. Both of them are right. The Abbey's door is open to you, keeper. Mind the draught.
bran
Monks owe us. Monks pay late. Still. It's a start.
That night a letter lies on the Command Table, weighed down with a smooth white stone. It says only: 'Thank you for counting them. Fondly, V.'
Under her name, in a different ink, someone has drawn a single black bar.

ch3_invitation.title: An Invitation
lines: A card arrives at the Command Table by barge, by pony and finally by a footman in a powdered wig who will not say who sent him. It is thick, gilt-edged and smells of violets.
velvette
Oh, darling. Look at this. A de Saulx card. I have not seen one since I was sixteen and singing for my supper at the bottom of their stairs.
surprised
velvette
'The Marquise de Saulx requests the pleasure of the company of the person who does not exist, at the Masquerade, which continues.' Which continues, she says. It has been a year.
bran
Who throws a party for a year?
velvette
The Causeway, mon vieux. They dance on the bridges while the ink lake comes up the steps. When the Blank came, they decided the music should simply not stop.
bran
And now a marquise wants the smudge. By name. Or by no name. That's worse.
Folded inside the card is a second sheet, unsigned, in a rough hand: 'The quay is going under. Somebody's singing it up. Come quick or don't bother.'
velvette
Two letters, one envelope. One of them is lying, and it is never the rough one.

ch3_quay_intro.title: Lantern Quay
lines: Lantern Quay is half gone. The white has bitten a hole through the middle of the wharf, and on the far side a crowd of dockhands and barge families is trapped against the water.
Across the gap, from nothing to nothing, runs a bridge of warm yellow light. A woman in a sequinned coat stands at the near end, singing at the top of her lungs.
saffron
Don't stop me! If I stop it goes, love, and they all go in the drink! Keep those things off me!
bran
She's singin' a bridge. Course she is. Why not.

ch3_quay_outro.title: Saffron Kiss
lines: The last barge child runs across the light, and the singer lets the final note go. The bridge goes out like a lamp. Nobody is on it.
saffron
Ha! Every one. Did you count? I counted. Forty-one and a goat.
saffron
Saffron Kiss, top of the bill at the Gilt Lantern till it fell in the lake. You'll be the one with no name. The whole quay's talking about you. Well, not talking. Sort of pointing.
saffron
Here's the thing, love. I can sing things up, but they don't stay. A bridge, a lamp, a door. They last as long as the song, and I've never finished a song in my life.
saffron
So I'm coming with you. You've got a town that stays put. I'd like to see what that's like.
happy

ch3_quay_after.title: Who Sent the Card
lines: saffron
The rough letter was mine. Sorry about the spelling. The posh one's from the Marquise. Everybody on the Causeway gets one eventually.
saffron
Here's what nobody prints. The masquerade has a host nobody's seen. Every night a few guests go up to pay their respects, and they don't come down again.
velvette
And the rest keep dancing. Of course they do. A missing guest is just more room on the floor.
saffron
The Marquise only lets in whoever sends the wine. If you want through the door, you'll want the Vauclair Terraces first. The presses up there feed the whole party.
bran
So we take a vineyard to go to a party to find out who's eatin' the guests. Lovely. Love a Tuesday.

ch3_masquerade_intro.title: The Masquerade
lines: The Velvet Causeway glitters across the ink lake, a city of bridges and balconies lit by ten thousand candles. Every window has music in it. Every step leading down to the water is a little shorter than last night.
A footman bows at the first bridge and hands Ash a plain white mask. He does not ask for a name.
saffron
Masks on, loves. Smile at everybody. If someone asks who you are, say you're a cousin. Everyone here is somebody's cousin.

ch3_hortense.title: The Marquise
lines: In the middle of the great hall a woman in blue silk is dancing with nobody. She sees Ash, stops dead in the middle of the floor, and the orchestra stops with her.
hortense
There you are. The person who does not exist. I have had your portrait drawn eleven times from descriptions, and every artist drew a different face. I see why.
smug
hortense
Hortense de Saulx. This is my party, technically. My family has hosted it for two hundred years, which mostly means paying for it.
hortense
Dance with me, sweet. Everyone is watching, and I would like them to see who I have caught.

reply: Oh. You lead. Nobody leads me. How refreshing. Let us go round once and give them something to talk about.
Good manners. Rarer than diamonds here, and worth more. Follow me, and mind my train.

choice.text: Stay where you are, watching the doors
reply: Watching the exits at a party. You and I are going to get on terribly well. Very wise, sweet. Somebody is about to need them.

ch3_verity_mask.title: A White Mask
lines: On the balcony above the hall, away from the candles, a woman in a cream robe and a plain white mask is watching the dancers with her hands folded.
verity
Hello again. Don't stop dancing on my account. I came to see whether the rumour was true.
verity
Something here eats guests. People assume it's mine. Everything hungry is assumed to be mine these days.
verity
It isn't. I have never sent anything to a party. I don't approve of parties. All that noise, and nobody writes anything down.
verity
Be careful who you dance with, Ash. This city has a great many masks, and some of them have been on so long there's nothing underneath.
When Ash looks up again, the balcony is empty, and the candle on its rail has burned straight down in a single moment.

ch3_course.title: The Next Course
lines: A bell rings somewhere above the hall. The music changes key. Half the dancers turn, all together, and their masks are smiling a little wider than masks should.
lantenay
Mesdames, messieurs. Our host calls for the next course. Do keep dancing, those of you who are not the course.
hortense
Lantenay, you old horror. Not tonight, and not my guest. Ash, sweet, the revellers have stopped being polite. Do the same.
angry

ch3_masquerade_outro.title: A Room in Hollowmark
lines: The hall is quiet. The orchestra has hidden under its music stands. The Duc de Lantenay has withdrawn, very slowly, upstairs.
hortense
Well. That is the most fun anyone has had at this party in a year, and I include the people who were eaten.
hortense
I'm coming with you to Hollowmark. Do not look so pleased. I need somewhere that is not here, and you need someone who knows which fork the Nobility stab each other with.
saffron
She's a liar, love. Everyone on the Causeway knows the Marquise is a liar.
hortense
Of course I am. Everyone here is. I'm only the best at it.
smug

ch3_masquerade_after.title: A Barge at Night
lines: saffron
Ash, love. The posh lot that went up to see the host, the ones who never came down. I've seen where the rest of them go.
saffron
There's a barge that ties up at Lantern Quay after midnight. No lights. Concord colours under the tarpaulin. It takes on crates of people in masks, and it sails for the Causeway's back stairs.
hortense
Gossip, sweet. The quay is full of it. I know a quicker way onto that wharf, if you insist on going. I insist on coming.
bran
She insists. She insists a lot. I don't like a woman who knows the quick way into a trap.
hortense
Bran, sweet. A trap is just a party you weren't told about.

ch3_wharf_intro.title: The Night Wharf
lines: Lantern Quay after midnight, every lamp out. A long black barge rides low at the end of the smugglers' wharf, and men in Concord grey are lifting crates aboard.
hortense
This way. Along the warehouses, keep to the dark side. Nobody looks at the dark side of anything here.
saffron
Hortense, how do you know the way to a Concord barge in the dark?
hortense
I know the way to everything in the dark, sweet. It's how I was raised.

ch3_gaudin.title: Delivery
lines: On the barge's deck, under a single hooded lantern, stands a steel table with straps on it. A neat card on the table reads: SUBJECT (UNREGISTERED). FOR THE ANATOMISTS OF THE OFFICE OF CORRECTIONS.
gaudin
Marquise. Punctual, and with the subject, as promised. The Office is very grateful. Your sister's notes will be marked paid in full.
Everyone turns to look at Hortense. She does not look away from Ash.
hortense

Yes. That's true. The Office sent me a letter the day after the Auditor fell, and I was to bring you here, and they would let Bérénice go. Every word I have said to you since was meant to get you onto this barge.
sad
bran
I said. I said she knew the quick way into a trap.

choice.text: Put a hand on your weapon
reply: Good. You should. I would think less of you otherwise. Now watch what I do with mine.

choice.text: Hold out your hand to her
reply: ...You are impossible. You know that? Here I am, ruining my own big scene, and you hold out your hand.

choice.text: Look at the steel table, then back at her
reply: Yes. I saw it too. I had imagined something with more velvet.

ch3_letter_aloud.title: The Concord's Letter
lines: Hortense takes a folded letter from her glove, breaks the Concord seal with her thumb and reads it aloud, in her best ballroom voice, to the whole wharf.
hortense
'To the Marquise de Saulx. The Office requires the unregistered subject, alive, for study. In return the debts of the House of de Saulx will be discharged, and the pupil Bérénice released.'
hortense
'Further: the Office will continue to supply the Causeway's host with guests from the debtors' rolls, so long as the Nobility keep the Blank off the bridges. Signed, for the Concord, Purser Gaudin.'
gaudin
Marquise, that letter was private.
hortense
Nothing on the Causeway is private, Purser. You fed debtors to that thing upstairs so the bridges would stay dry, and you wrote it down. The Concord always writes it down.
angry
She tears the letter in two and lets the pieces go into the ink lake.
hortense
I will fetch my sister myself. Ash, sweet. Shall we sink a barge?

ch3_wharf_outro.title: Odds
lines: The Concord barge lists, groans and settles into the ink with its steel table still on deck. The crates on the wharf are open. Inside, blinking, are debtors from half the towns on the lake.
bran
So. She was sellin' you. To the Concord. For cuttin' up.
hortense
I was. I am not any more. I changed my mind somewhere around the first dance, and then I changed it back four times, and then I saw the table.
hortense
Keep me or throw me in the lake. I would do either in your place. But if you keep me, I will be the most useful liar you ever had, and I shall only lie to other people.
velvette
Darling, a confession on a sinking barge. It has everything. I could not have staged it better.
smug
Ash looks at Hortense for a while, then hands her back her rapier, hilt first.
hortense
...Thank you. I shall try very hard to deserve that. It will be a novelty.
sad

ch3_wharf_after.title: The Host
lines: hortense
Here is the rest of it. The thing upstairs at the masquerade came to the first night after the Blank arrived. Nobody invited it. It sat down at the head of the table and never left.
hortense
It is mostly mouth. It eats guests, and while it's eating, the ink stays off the bridges. The Nobility worked that out in a week. The Concord worked out who to send.
saffron
So everyone dances, and every night a few go upstairs, and the city stays dry. That's the party. That's the whole party.
hortense
Lantenay holds the stairs. He won't open the hall to people the Nobility despise. Make them merely dislike you, and I can get us up.

ch3_two_rapiers.title: Two Rapiers
lines: The practice yard behind the barracks, early. Fauvette is already there, rapier out, when Hortense arrives in a borrowed fencing jacket that fits her suspiciously well.
velvette
Marquise. I sang at your family's masquerade when I was sixteen. Bottom of the stairs, by the coats. You paid the Encore double to have me there.
hortense
I remember. You were very good. You were also stealing from the coats.
velvette
Every coat in the house, chérie. I still have a glove of your father's. It is the only de Saulx thing I own that was paid for.
hortense
Then we are even. I knew whose guests went upstairs and did not come back, and I went on dancing. You knew the Encore's volunteers, and you went on bowing. We are both very good at going on.
velvette
Hm. Fine. One bout. First to touch three times. If I win, you stop calling me 'the cabaret girl'.
hortense
And if I win?
velvette
You won't, darling. But if you do, I'll give you back the glove.
smug
They salute. Nobody in Hollowmark gets any work done for an hour. The score, according to Fauvette, is three to two. According to Hortense, it is also three to two, the other way round.

ch3_shallows_intro.title: Pendower Shallows
lines: On the mud flats of Pendower Shallows, a dozen word-fishers are crowded round a woman with a folding table, three walnut shells and a very loud voice.
nan
Find the word, win the word! Under one of these shells, a genuine 'tomorrow', fresh off the nets this morning. Sixpence a go! Who's feeling lucky? You, sir, with the face!
Her shadow stretches across the mud in the wrong direction, away from the sun. It clears its throat.
tally
The word is not under any of the shells. It is in her sleeve. It has been in her sleeve since Monday.
nan
Tally!
The word-fishers turn as one. Behind them, out on the shallows, the ink starts to boil with eels.

ch3_shallows_outro.title: Nan Cripps and Tally
lines: nan
Well! That was a lovely bit of teamwork. I distracted them, you hit them, Tally ruined my livelihood. Shall we do it again tomorrow?
tally
She signed me over to a moneylender when she was fifteen. Her conscience, as collateral. It came out like this. Talking.
nan
Tally's very honest. It's a terrible burden. I'm Nan, by the way. Nan Cripps. You'll be the one with no name. That's a lovely trick, that is. I'd pay to learn it.
nan
I hear Hollowmark's got a market and nobody who knows how to fleece it. Take me on. I'll work cheap, and Tally will make sure I'm telling the truth about the cheap part.
tally
She will not work cheap.

host_intro.title: The Head of the Table
lines: Above the great hall, behind doors of black lacquer, is the banqueting room. The table runs the length of the room. Every chair is empty except the one at the far end.
The guest at the head of the table is enormous, and wears a mask on every part of it that could be called a face. Most of it is mouth.
host
AH. THE LATE ARRIVALS. SIT, SIT. THERE IS ALWAYS ROOM AT THE TABLE. THERE IS ALWAYS ROOM INSIDE.
hortense
Good evening, monsieur. I'm afraid we're here to end the party.
host
NOBODY ENDS THE PARTY. THE PARTY ENDS WHEN THE GUESTS RUN OUT. AND THE GUESTS NEVER RUN OUT.

host_phase2.title: Second Helpings
lines: The Host tears off its masks one after another and throws them aside. Under each one is another mouth.
host
RUDE. RUDE GUESTS. I WILL EAT THE TABLE. I WILL EAT THE FLOOR. I WILL EAT THE BRIDGES AND THE LAKE CAN HAVE WHAT IS LEFT.
saffron
It's going to jump, love! Watch where its shadow lands!

host_outro.title: The Party Ends
lines: The Host sits back in its chair. All its mouths close at once. Slowly, the way a candle goes, it is gone, and the chair at the head of the table is just a chair.
From the hall below comes a sound nobody on the Causeway has heard in a year: the orchestra stopping, and not starting again.
hortense
There. The party is over. My family hosted it for two hundred years, and I have ended it in one evening. Grandmère would be appalled.
happy
saffron
Listen to that. Quiet. You can hear the water.
bran
You can hear the water comin' up the steps.
hortense
Yes. Now the Causeway has to keep itself dry the ordinary way, with walls, and work, and you. How dreadful for them.

ch3_end.title: The Party's Over
lines: The masquerade is over. On the Causeway the candles are out and the masks are off, and people are standing on the bridges looking at each other's faces as if they had never seen them before.
lantenay
The Nobility will remember this, Keeper. Some of us with gratitude. Most of us with a great deal of paperwork. Our wine still goes to whoever holds the presses.
hortense
He means thank you. The Nobility have no word for it, so they send wine.
saffron
I'm writing a song about tonight. I'm going to finish it. You see if I don't.
That night a letter lies on the Command Table, weighed down with a white mask. It says only: 'That one was not mine. Someone else is setting places at the table. Fondly, V.'
Under her name, in a different ink, someone has drawn two black bars.

ch4_tide.title: A Piece of the Sea
lines: A fishing boat comes up the Hollowmark road on a cart, pulled by four men and a donkey. It is dry inside. There is a wave in it.
The wave stands in the boat like a sheet of green glass, curled over at the top, with a crab halfway up it, stopped in the act of falling.
pascoe
Loveday Pascoe, harbourmaster at Trevail. That's the sea, that is. A bit of it. We cut a piece off to show you, since nobody up here would believe us.
bran
You cut a bit off the sea.
surprised
pascoe
Saw, chisel, three days. It don't move and it don't drip. Five nights back the whole bay stopped mid-wave, and the boats out past the bar kept sailing, on into the white.
pascoe
The Moot says ask the town with nobody in charge. The Moot reckons nobody might know what to do about nothing.
bran
That's us. Nobody, at your service. Rates on request.
smug
The crab moves one leg. Everyone pretends not to see it.

ch4_harbour_intro.title: Trevail Harbour
lines: Trevail is a harbour town built up a cliff, and over all of it, roofs, chapel and quay, hangs a wave. It is green at the bottom and white at the top, and it has been about to fall for five days.
Under it the town has carried on. Washing hangs from its underside on hooks. A boy is fishing up into it with a bent pin.
pascoe
Mind your heads. She don't fall, but she's cold to brush against, and she gets in your hair.
pascoe
Thirty-two boats were out past the bar when she stopped. They'm still sailing, look, out there. Sailing for home and getting further off.
pascoe
The bell's how we call boats in, fog or night. If I ring it, some of them might hear and come about. Only the sea's walked up the slipway in pieces, and it don't like the bell.

ch4_harbour_outro.title: Eleven Home
lines: The bell goes for a long time. Out past the bar, small and far off, sails turn. Eleven boats come about and come in under the wave, slowly, the crews looking up at it with their mouths open.
pascoe
Eleven. Out of thirty-two.
She writes it in the harbour book: eleven home, twenty-one out. She does not write 'lost'. Trevail has a word for boats still sailing, and it is 'out'.
pascoe

There's a thing at Halfwave you should see. The chapel there kept a looking-glass for the drowned, so they could find their faces. Since the sea stopped there's a knight in it. She talks. Mostly about herself.
pascoe
And Polgarrow Light's gone dark. The keeper's still up there, Jory Hocking. He keeps saying things, his girl says. Not in his own voice.

ch4_harbour_after.title: Pilchards and a Chart
lines: bran
Eleven boats. The Moot's sent a barrel of pilchards and a letter sayin' they're in our debt. I've framed the letter. I've eaten the pilchards.
Quill has pinned a coast chart to the Command Table. Halfwave Bay is shaded where the sea stopped short of the shore: a long white line where the tide should be.
quill
Halfwave Bay. Unclaimed, unregistered, and per the harbourmaster, haunted by a knight in a looking-glass. I have filed it under 'other'.
quill
The chapel stands on the beach. If we want to look in that glass, the bay will have to be ours first. Nobody at Halfwave lets strangers onto the sand since the drowned started walking out of it.

ch4_mirror_intro.title: Halfwave Bay
lines: At Halfwave the sea stopped short of the beach. Twenty yards out the tide stands up in a long green wall, and fish hang in it like flies in amber. The sand between is dry and full of footprints that point the wrong way.
Up the beach is a chapel with no roof. From inside it, someone is talking.
ilse
...and then she said, the tide will come back, and Ilse said, it would not dare. Is somebody out there? Ilse can hear boots.
bran
There's a woman in that chapel talkin' about 'erself. In the third person. On a Tuesday.

ch4_ilse.title: The Knight in the Glass
lines: On the chapel's back wall hangs a tall looking-glass in a frame of driftwood, salt-white to the elbow. In it stands a knight in silvered armour, with a spear, her helmet under her arm, and nobody in the chapel for her to be the reflection of.
ilse
At last. An audience. Turn round, let her look at you. Hm. No face to speak of. You will do.
smug
ilse
Ilse. Dame Ilse, if anyone is still counting. The woman who owned this face looked into this glass every Sunday. Then the Blank took her off the beach, and it forgot to take the reflection.
ilse
So here Ilse is, everything back to front. She parts her hair on the wrong side and she cannot read a word of the hymn board.
The tideline groans. Through the chapel door the green wall bulges, and white shapes start to climb out of it.
ilse
Ah. The verger and his friends. They come for the glass every night. Ilse would rather they did not break it, as she is still inside it.

choice.text: Hold out your hand to the glass
reply: Bold. She likes bold. Wait there.
Her gauntlet comes out of the mirror the way a hand comes out of water. Then the rest of her, armour, spear and all. The glass behind her is empty.
Yes, good, guard her. She will see to the rest herself.
Behind Ash there is a sound like someone stepping out of a pond. When Ash looks back, the knight is standing in the chapel and the glass is empty.

ch4_mirror_outro.title: Dame Ilse
lines: The last salt wight goes down in a spray of white grit. Ilse stands over the heap with her spear, admiring the angle she is standing at.
ilse
The glass held. Good. If it breaks, she does not know what happens to her, and she would rather not find out in front of people.
ilse
Now. She has spent a week in a chapel with nothing to look at but fish. You have a town. Does it have mirrors?
bran
It's got a puddle outside the tavern.
ilse
Then Ilse will make do. She is told she is very good at making do. She was told it backwards, but the meaning came through.
happy

ch4_mirror_after.title: The Keeper's Daughter
lines: A girl in a sou'wester is waiting at the Hollowmark gate with a lantern that is not lit. She has walked from Polgarrow, which is forty miles.
kerra
Kerra Hocking. Me dad keeps Polgarrow Light. Kept. It went out the night the sea stopped, and he won't come down.
kerra
He talks all night. Only 'tis not his talk. There's gaps in it, like someone took a knife to the words. And he says your name. The one you haven't got.
ilse
A man who speaks in gaps. How dull for him. Ilse will come, naturally.
kerra
Halfwave's got nobody watching it now the drowned are walking. Put somebody in charge there and I'll take you up the Light. I won't leave the village to look after itself.

ch4_light_intro.title: Polgarrow Light
lines: Polgarrow Light stands on a black rock at the end of the land. The lamp is dark. Below it the sea has stopped in the middle of breaking over the rock, and the spray stands in a white fan, every drop in place.
kerra
Mind the spray. 'Tis like walking through a bead curtain, only it cuts.
kerra
The gannets nest up top. Since the sea stopped there's only half of each one. They still dive. Don't stand where their shadow stops.
ilse
Half a bird. Ilse sympathises. She is half a person, and she has never looked better.
smug

ch4_keeper.title: The Keeper's Voice
lines: The lamp room is cold. Jory Hocking sits by the dark lamp in his oilskins, very upright, hands on his knees. His clothes are wet, as if he has just come up out of the sea. He has not been in the sea for five days.
kerra
Dad. 'Tis me. I've brought the one with no name, like you kept saying.
keeper
Kerra. Good maid. Stand by the door.
He turns his head to Ash. His mouth keeps moving after his face has stopped.
vacancy
[[You]] [[were]] [[on]] [[the]] [[plate]]. [[You]] [[were]] [[not]] [[finished]]. back.
vacancy
[[The]] [[sea]] [[is]] [[in]] [[the]] [[larder]]. [[The]] [[tide]] [[is]] [[a]] [[crumb]]. supper [[soon]].
vacancy
[[Every]] [[name]] [[on]] [[the]] [[shelf]]. [[One]] [[left]] [[out]]. door [[open]].
ilse
That is no man talking. That is a hole talking through a man. Ilse knows the difference. She is the other way round.
vacancy
[[Glass]] [[girl]]. [[You]] [[were]] [[left]] [[on]] [[the]] [[side]]. later.
Ilse takes one step back from the keeper, and for a moment, in the black window behind her, she has no reflection at all.
kerra
Light the lamp! He's better in the light. He was always better in the light.

ch4_light_outro.title: Five Days
lines: The lamp catches. A beam goes out over the stopped sea, and for the first time in five days the spray on the rock glitters instead of just hanging there.
Jory Hocking blinks at the light, then at his daughter, then at the wet sleeves of his own coat.
keeper
Kerra? What day is it? I was in the middle of telling somebody something. Long story. Couldn't get to the end of it.
kerra
Five days, Dad. You've been talking five days.
keeper
Have I? Then I'm dry. Put the kettle on, maid.
He cannot remember a word of it. Kerra can, all of it. On the way down the rock she asks whether Hollowmark wants a diver, because she is not going to sit at home and listen to him not remember.

ch4_light_after.title: Three Words
lines: quill
Item: one lighthouse, relit. Item: one keeper, dry. Item: one diver, Kerra Hocking, signed on, wages in pilchards, per her own terms.
quill
Item: the keeper's words, as his daughter remembers them. I wrote them down. Half the page came out black.
He turns the ledger round. Where he wrote the keeper's words, the ink has run together into thick black bars, neat as a censor's. Three words are left clear: 'back', 'supper', 'door'.
quill
I used my good ink, as well.

ch4_verity.title: Elsewhere
lines: Elsewhere. In a room with no windows, Verity Hale is marking a map of the Inklands in chalk, the way she has every evening for two years. A ring here, where the Blank will go next. A line there, where it should stop.
There is a ring on the coast. She did not draw it. She looks at her chalk, and then at her fingers. They are clean.
verity
Polgarrow. I have never once aimed at Polgarrow. There is nothing there that needs a clean page. A lighthouse and some very stubborn fish.
verity
Halfwave. Trevail. I did not draw these either. I should think I would remember.
She takes a fresh sheet and begins a letter. 'Dear Ash. I believe I owe you an explanation.' She reads it twice.
Then she folds it, holds it in the candle until it is gone, and draws a neat chalk ring round Polgarrow herself, so that the map is correct again.
verity
There. My mistake.

lowwater_intro.title: Low Water
lines: At the bottom of the bay the water has gathered itself into one shape, taller than a house, green and full of wrecks. A ship's figurehead turns in it like a face. Things that drowned move behind its skin.
pascoe
That's her. Everything the tide forgot to bring back. My grandad's boat's in there, look. Second from the top.
ilse
It is looking at her. Ilse knows when she is being looked at. It wants to come in, and it cannot remember where in is.
Low Water leans up the bay towards the shore it lost, and the sand begins to move.

lowwater_phase2.title: High Water
lines: Low Water rears up and the sea bed shakes. Far up the bay, the standing wall of the tide groans and leans.
pascoe
Tide's turning! Get up on the high banks, quick, where the sand's pale!

lowwater_outro.title: The Tide Comes Home
lines: Low Water comes apart. The wrecks drop out of it onto the sea bed one by one, with a sound like furniture. Then the water runs out of the shape and down the bay, and keeps running, and does not stop.
Far up the beach, the standing wall of the tide shivers. A fish drops out of it, flaps on the sand, and looks surprised.
pascoe
She's moving. Look at her. Slow as cold treacle, but she's moving.
ilse
And Ilse has saved the bay. You helped. Somebody make a note.
happy

ch4_end.title: One Black Bar More
lines: By the time the party is back in Hollowmark the news has come up the road ahead of it: at Halfwave the tide moved a hand's width in a day. At Trevail two more boats came in out of the white.
pascoe
The Moot's voted. Hollowmark's welcome in every harbour on the coast, and pays half for pilchards. 'Tis the highest honour we've got.
ilse
Ilse has found a mirror in the town hall that shows her the right way round. She has been standing in front of it for an hour. She recommends it.
That night there is no letter on the Command Table. Quill checks twice. It is the first chapter of all this that has ended without one from Verity Hale.
In the dust where the letter would be, someone has drawn three black bars with a finger.

Meet the tithe column at Old Mill Crossing (territory map) once Hollowmark holds 4 provinces and has 8 Renown.
New story mission: The Auditor
Stop him on the Tithe Road. Build an Infirmary and reach 15 Renown first.
Act 1 complete: The Unregistered Town
Verity Hale has made her offer. The fog has lifted over Saint Ledger's Abbey, in the north. Hold six provinces and the north will send for you.
Chapter 2: The Copying Monks
New story mission: The Wax Barges. Candleford, on the lake in the north (territory map).
New story mission: The Copying Hall
Saint Ledger's Abbey (territory map). Prioress Ebba will meet you at the gate.

The Bonefield Cloister, held by the Erasers (territory map). Find Sister Osyth.
New story mission: The Abbot Who Copied Himself
Saint Ledger's Abbey. The Prioress opens the hall once the Abbey is at least Neutral with you (Diplomacy).
Chapter 2 complete: The Copying Monks
The Abbey's door is open and the Erasers know your name. The north is yours to hold until the Causeway calls. New goals are in the journal.
Chapter 3: Masquerade
New story mission: The Singer on the Quay. Lantern Quay, on the ink lake in the south-west (territory map).

The Velvet Causeway (territory map). The door opens for whoever holds the Vauclair Terraces.
New story mission: The Night Wharf
Lantern Quay (territory map), after midnight.

The Velvet Causeway. Lantenay opens the stairs once the Velvet Nobility are at least Neutral with you (Diplomacy).

The music has stopped on the Causeway and the Concord knows Hortense's name. The lake is yours to hold until the sea calls. New goals are in the journal.
Chapter 4: The Sea Stops
New story mission: The Wave at Trevail. Trevail Harbour, on the coast in the south-east (territory map).
New story mission: The Knight in the Glass
Halfwave Bay (territory map). Claim the bay first: the chapel stands on its beach.
New story mission: The Keeper's Light
Polgarrow Light (territory map). Put a governor in Halfwave Bay first: Kerra will not leave the village unwatched.
New story mission: Low Water
Halfwave Bay (territory map). The Harbour Moot will row you out onto the sea bed once they are at least Neutral with you (Diplomacy).
Chapter 4 complete: The Sea Stops
The tide is coming home to Halfwave a hand's width a day, and the coast knows Ilse's name. Hold the south-east until the capital calls. New goals are in the journal.
